evidence: Cic. Lael. 17: sine ūllā exceptiōne (Lewis & Short)
terms.comment: Lewis & Short: good prose and very frequent, especially in Cicero, most often in sine (ūllā) exceptiōne and cum exceptiōne. In law it is the defendant’s plea against the plaintiff’s claim.

terms.gloss: make an exception of, leave out
evidence: Cic. Cat. 4.15: hōsce ego hominēs excipiō et sēcernō libenter (Lewis & Short)
Hor. Ep. 1.10.50: exceptō quod, except that (Lewis & Short)
terms.comment: Its everyday senses are others: to catch (a ball), to receive or welcome (a guest), to follow on. The ablative absolute exceptō or exceptā with a noun means “with the exception of” (see except).

phrases.latin: cōnsiliōrum, voluntātum sine ūllā exceptiōne commūnitās
phrases.english: a sharing of plans and wishes without any exception

phrases.latin: hōsce ego hominēs excipiō et sēcernō libenter
phrases.english: these men I gladly make an exception of and set apart

phrases.latin: exceptō quod nōn simul essēs, cētera laetus
phrases.english: happy in everything else, except that you were not with me

phrases.latin: Hodiē tē excipiam: post cēnam lūdere licet.
phrases.english: Today I’ll make an exception for you: you may play after supper.
